b.bio: The name as printed here belongs to a Latin patristic or early medieval author represented in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 95 by a two-page Admonition. No surviving record describes this person: the sources concern two later Italians of the same name — an eighteenth-century jurist and classical scholar (Orazio Filippo Bianchi) and a Baroque painter — neither of whom can be identified with the author of the PL 95 text. Nothing beyond the library record is known about this author.
b.s: The library holds only his brief Admonition (PL 95), a short exhortatory text whose attribution and context rest solely on that printing.

b.bio: Octavius Fraga Frangipanus appears here only as the author of two short pieces printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 46: a foreword and a letter addressed to Pope Pius VII. Both concern the editorial question of which ancient sermons may be attributed to Augustine: he defends attribution on the basis of manuscript evidence, cites the Vienna codex as confirming the authenticity of the Cassinese collection, dates Lombard-character codices to the tenth or eleventh century, and notes that Cassinese codices were transcribed under abbots Theobald and Desiderius. He writes against the monk editors, faulting them for consulting only two Italian libraries and for scholars' lack of time with the codices, and draws on Mabillon, Combefis, Vallarsi, Bandini, Bruni, Verlinus, Vinding, and Aloysius Vincentius Cassittus. No surviving record gives his life dates or offices.
b.s: His pieces here are documentary evidence for early nineteenth-century debates over the manuscript tradition behind the Augustinian sermon collections, not theological treatises.

b.bio: Ottmar Luscinius (Nachtgall), an Alsatian humanist born in Strasbourg, studied under Jacob Wimppheling, then in Paris Latin under Faustus Andrelini and Greek under Hieronymus Aleander, then canon law at Louvain, Padua, and Vienna, where he also studied music under Wolfgang Grefinger. After travels in Greece and Asia Minor he returned to Strasbourg in 1514. In 1515 he was appointed organist at St. Thomas and received a vicariate as a priest; he also taught in the school of the Knights Hospitallers and the cathedral school. He published Greek manuals, an edition of Lucian with translation, the Institutiones musicae (1515), and a revised edition of Trovamala's Rosella (1516). Sources differ on his birth year: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1487, Wikipedia 1478–1480; he died at Freiburg in 1537.
b.s: The work held here is his 1518 edition of the Commentary on the Pauline Epistles then ascribed to Bishop Haimo of Halberstadt (PL 117). Its introduction condemns scholastic disputation (naming Thomists, Scotists, and Occamists) and champions Scripture alone as the surest path to wisdom and beatitude.

b.bio: The library's author is Odalric the provost, an eleventh-century canon (provost) of Reims known chiefly as donor of manuscript 15 of the Bibliothèque municipale de Reims, a tripartite psalter from the Reims scriptorium whose necrological notices record his liturgical memory. He must not be confused with his namesake Odalric, Archbishop of Reims from a Lotharingian family who held that see from 962 to 969 and appears in Flodoard's annals; another namesake is associated with a report on a translation legend of Pope Clement's relics in the mid-eleventh century. The single page held here is a brief polemic pronouncing excommunication on thieves of church goods.
b.s: His one-page sentence against sacrilegious persons shows how an eleventh-century Reims canon grounded ecclesiastical sanction in apostolic and saintly authority, barring offenders from the eucharist and Christian society.

b.bio: Odalric the Provost was an eleventh-century ecclesiastic at Reims, the subject of a 2015 colloquium volume on him and Reims municipal manuscript 15. He is not to be confused with Odalric, archbishop of Reims (962–969), or with Odolric, abbot of Saint-Martial at Limoges (died c. 1040). The library holds a single-page Testament under his name in PL 150, a citation-survey and history arguing against simoniacal acquisition of ministries.
b.s: His Testament is a brief eleventh-century witness against simony, insisting that offices gained illicitly be restored lest divine vengeance follow and that canonical prebends be fully observed.

b.bio: None of the surviving records describes an Odo of Reims; they cover Odo of Glanfeuil (9th-century abbot and hagiographer), Odo of Deuil (crusade historian, d. 1162), and Odo of Cluny (d. 942), all different men, so they cannot be used for this note. The works held under this name are a charter, an epistle, and a letter to Count Thomas, printed in PL 172. The charter grants a monastery to the Carthusians free of taxation, secures future acquisitions by gift or purchase in perpetuity, invokes papal privilege for monastic property rights, threatens violators with anathema, and appeals to saints as able to obtain great things from divine omnipotence. It cites Pope Innocent II, placing the text in his pontificate (1130–1143).
b.s: The texts here are property documents: evidence of how a 12th-century archbishopric secured Carthusian endowments through privilege and anathema.

b.bio: the surviving records describe a different man: Odilo of Cluny (c. 962–1049), fifth abbot of Cluny. None of them concerns this author, and the works held here do not fit him. The library's texts are a treatise on the translation of relics, sermons, and an epistle, all tied to the abbey of Saint-Médard at Soissons: they defend the presence of Gregory's body there against doubters, recount Charles the Bald's translation of saints' bodies to Soissons, cite Emperor Louis and Abbot Hilduin, and polemicize against Ostrold of Lyons and Warimbert, bishop of Suessiones. The author is an Odilo connected with Saint-Médard and its traditions; his dates and offices are not established by any source given.
b.s: His translation treatise is a primary witness to how Carolingian Soissons claimed and defended its relic collections, including the contested resting place of Gregory at Saint-Médard.

b.bio: the surviving records here do not describe an 'Odo of Auch'. They cover three different medieval authors named Odo: a ninth-century Benedictine abbot and hagiographer of Glanfeuil and Saint-Maur-des-Fossés (sources 1–2), Odo of Deuil (d. 1162), chaplain to Louis VII on the Second Crusade (source 3), and Odo of Canterbury (d. 1200), abbot of Battle (source 4). None is connected with Auch or with the work held under this name. The library's single item, a two-page letter addressed to Garcia of Auch printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 137, treats the Church, sacraments, Scripture, and law in historical form; it alone determines who this author is taken to be.
b.s: The library holds only his Letter to Garcia of Auch (PL 137), a brief historical treatment of the Church, sacraments, Scripture, and law.

w: Charter of Saint Vigor of Bayeux

b.bio: Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror, was made bishop of Bayeux in 1049 and after the Conquest became Earl of Kent and William's chief administrator in England. He is probably the commissioner of the Bayeux Tapestry. Tried for defrauding the royal government, he fell from favor, was freed on William's deathbed, and died at Palermo in 1097 while traveling toward crusade. The library holds under his name a single charter concerning Saint Vigor of Bayeux, an act of episcopal administration rather than theology.
b.s: The charter here documents his governance of the Bayeux diocese; readers of his name should note he is known as a bishop-patron and administrator, not as a theological author.

b.bio: Odo (Eudes) of Beauvais was a West Frankish prelate: abbot of Corbie from 852 or at least before April 853, then bishop of Beauvais from around 860 until his death on 28 January 881. He served the Carolingian court as a diplomat on missions to East Francia and Rome, defended Corbie against Viking raiders under Weland in 859, and worked closely with Ratramnus of Corbie. He wrote a lost treatise on Easter in opposition to Greek practice.
b.s: The works held here are his Passion of Saint Lucian — the first text to portray Lucian as founding bishop of Beauvais — together with short canons and an institution. The sermon presents martyrdom as Christ's own victory renewed in each martyr (Christ conquers again in each martyr's victory), portrays martyrs as filling up what is lacking to Christ's sufferings, and holds that praising martyrs edifies the whole church.

b.bio: Odo of Canterbury (Odo Cantianus), probably a native of Kent, became a monk at Christ Church, Canterbury. He was sub-prior in 1163 and was sent by Thomas Becket to Pope Alexander III as proctor in the dispute over the Archbishop of York's carrying the cross in the southern province. In 1167 he became prior. Until Becket's murder he seems to have wavered between king and archbishop, but then took a decided stand for ecclesiastical authority against royal encroachment. On 1 September 1172 his convent put him forward as worthy of the archbishopric, though the king procrastinated and no result followed. On 19 July 1175 he was elected abbot of Battle. John of Salisbury's 'Entheticus' praises him as wholly devoted to books that breathe Christ. His writings are hard to separate from those of Odo of Cheriton and Odo of Murimund.
b.s: The works held here are conciliar and synodal documents defending church property, episcopal discipline, and the subordination of kings to bishops holding the keys — the program he served under Becket.

b.bio: A monk of the abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés who spent his youth there, was forced to flee the abbey at some point, and returned to it around 1058 after a stay at Saint-Maur-sur-Loire; he served as copyist and scholasticus. He is not the ninth-century abbot Odo of Glanfeuil, another writer associated with the same house and its Life of St. Maurus; only one writing by this later Odo survives. His Life of Count Burchard of Melun preserves details on the origin of the abbey of Fosses.
b.s: His single surviving work, the Life of Burchard held here, is a principal source for the founding of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés and its reform under Cluniac observance.

b.bio: the surviving records here describe a different man: Odo of Cambrai (also called Odo of Tournai or Odoardus), born at Orléans, monk and abbot of Saint-Martin at Tournai, bishop of Cambrai from 1105/6, exiled in 1110, dead at Anchin in 1113. He cannot be the author of the work this library holds: his death predates the Waldensian movement, which the synodal statutes under this name denounce. No surviving record identifies the Odo of Toul who issued these statutes, so nothing can be asserted about his life, dates, or office.
b.s: The single work held here is a set of synodal statutes disciplining plunderers of church goods and the Waldensian heretics, with rules on suspension of services where plundered goods rest, Sunday proclamation of named excommunications, satisfaction beyond restitution before absolution, and burial during interdict.

w: On the Expedition of Louis VII to the East
On the Expedition to the East

b.bio: Odo of Deuil (also Odon de Deuil, Odo de Deogilo), born at Deuil in the valley of Montmorency to a modest family, was a monk of Saint-Denis and confidant of Abbot Suger. He accompanied Louis VII on the Second Crusade as the king's chaplain and secretary. On his return Suger made him abbot of Saint-Corneille de Compiègne; after Suger's death in 1151 he was recalled by the monks of Saint-Denis to govern their congregation, where his tenure saw disputes over domains with the archbishop of Bourges and the bishop of Beauvais. He died in 1162.
b.s: His De profectione Ludovici VII in Orientem is a firsthand day-by-day account of the Second Crusade from France to Antioch, written as material for Suger's planned biography of Louis VII, and it blames the crusade's failure on human action — above all the Byzantines under Manuel Comnenus — rather than divine will.

b.bio: Odo de Soliaco (Eudes de Sully) was bishop of Paris from 1197 until his death in 1208. He came into conflict with Philip II over the king's attempted repudiation of his wife, continued the building of Notre-Dame, and promoted the elevation of the host at Mass and polyphonic music, including that of Pérotin. He regulated cathedral celebrations such as Christmas and the Feast of Fools, tried to ban chess, forbade communion for children, and founded the abbey that became Port-Royal. The works held here are his statutes and pious donations, synodal constitutions, and a report of a miracle.
b.s: His synodal statutes are among the earliest episcopal legislation on liturgical practice in Paris, including the abolition of the Feast of Fools and reform of corrupted liturgy by episcopal authority.

b.bio: Olegarius Bonestruga was born in Barcelona in 1060 to a noble family. He entered the cathedral canons of Barcelona as a child, became deacon (1089) and dean (1094), then prior of Saint-Adrian (1099) and abbot of Saint-Ruf in Avignon (1113). He was elected Bishop of Barcelona around 1116 (Catholic-Hierarchy gives 1115, marked uncertain) and appointed Archbishop of Tarragona on 21 March 1118 with the task of restoring that metropolitanate. He attended reform councils at Toulouse and Reims (1119), the First Lateran Council (1123), and Clermont (1130), and served as crusade legate in Spain. He was canonised in 1675.
b.s: The works held here are a charter and two letters — to Raymond, bishop of Ausona, and to Pope Innocent II — treating sin, grace, and whether a man who has killed accidentally may receive minor orders, arguing that uncertain things are interpreted in the better part.

w: Consecration of the Church of Vic
Sermon on the feast of St. Narcissus
Synodal letter of the Council of Narbonne

b.bio: Oliba was born c. 971 into the comital family of Besalú-Cerdanya in the Spanish March, great-grandson of Wilfred the Hairy. He ruled the counties of Berga and Ripoll from 988, renounced them around 1002/1003 to become a monk at Ripoll, and later served as abbot of Santa Maria de Ripoll and Sant Miquel de Cuixà and as bishop of Vic from 1017 or 1018 until his death in 1046. He founded the monastery of Santa Maria de Montserrat and is regarded as the founder of the Truce of God. The works held here — letters, a consecration sermon for the church of Vic, a life of St. Afra, a synodal letter of the Council of Narbonne, and a sermon on St. Narcissus — match this bishop-abbot.
b.s: One of the most important prelates of eleventh-century Iberia and considered a spiritual founder of Catalonia; his letters and sermons here show him defending ecclesiastical discipline: forbidding marriage within forbidden degrees, condemning divination and augury, and opposing usurpers of St. Peter's estates.

w: Life, election, and deeds of Saint Gregory VII

b.bio: Panvinio was born at Verona (sources give 23 or 24 February, in 1529 or 1530) and entered the Augustinians at eleven. He studied in Naples and Rome, took a doctorate in theology in 1557, and served Cardinal Alessandro Farnese as librarian and as corrector and reviser of the books of the Vatican Library. A prolific historian and antiquary, he wrote on Roman fasti, revised Platina's Lives of the Popes, and compiled a chronicle of his order. Sources differ on his death date (7 or 27 April 1568); he died at Palermo while accompanying Cardinal Farnese toward the Synod of Monreale.
b.s: The work held here is his Life, election, and deeds of Saint Gregory VII, a historical-polemical account of the papal election dispute that draws on witnesses such as Benno; the mined text asserts both that the emperor holds a right to elect the pope and that papal election belongs freely to the Roman church, and it argues against both Emperor Henry IV and Gregory VII/Hildebrand on different points.

b.bio: A cleric at the court of Alfonso VI of León, possibly his chaplain; some authors think he was foreign, perhaps arriving with Queen Constance. After the king banished Bishop Pedro Núñez in 1080, Osmund was designated to the see of Astorga (the cathedra of Santo Toribio). During his pontificate he recovered church properties that had been usurped during poor administration and received royal gifts and tribute grants for his diocese. The sources give no birth or death dates.
b.s: The single work held here is a letter to Ida recounting how disciples carried Marian relics to Spain in persecution and how bishops fleeing the Saracens brought them to Asturias, with King Alfonso authenticating the relic charter by his own hand — an eleventh-century witness to Spanish relic traditions.

b.bio: Othelbold was a monk of the abbey of Saint Bavo in Ghent who wrote in defense of that community's cult of its patron. His letter to the noblewoman Otgiva answers holders of relics at Liège, Soissons, and elsewhere who claimed parts of Saint Bavo, arguing that the saint's body belongs to Ghent because God confirmed it there by miracles and because the abbey's authority rests on apostolic privilege. The letter cites Abbot Odwin and Emperor Otto, and draws on an earlier life of Bavo and a book of the saints' deeds.
b.s: His letter is an early witness to medieval disputes over the division of saints' relics and to the claim that a monastery's right to its patron's body is grounded in divine confirmation rather than mere possession.

b.bio: A monk and cleric of St. Emmeram in Regensburg, Otker is known through a short musical treatise preserved in a Munich manuscript (Clm 4622) of Bavarian origin. In it he presents a measurement of the monochord derived from a four-part figure, which he names a 'theorema troporum' — a 'sieve of the monochord' ('cribrum monocordi'). He should not be confused with his better-documented fellow monk Otloh of St. Emmeram (c. 1010–c. 1072), whose works are different in kind.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief technical definition relating monochord measurement to Guido's teaching, surviving in manuscript and early modern editions (Le Pez 1721–1729, Gerbert 1784, Mettenleiter 1866).

b.bio: Otto was born around 1060 or 1061 into a noble family of Swabia (the Mistelbach descent is possible but unproven). He served in the Polish ducal household under Judith of Swabia, entered Emperor Henry IV's service in 1090, and became imperial chancellor early in 1102. Henry IV appointed him Bishop of Bamberg on 25 December 1102; disputes with Henry V and the metropolitan of Mainz delayed his consecration until 13 May 1106, by Pope Paschal II at Anagni. He received the pallium in Rome on 15 April 1111 after accompanying Henry V there, helped prepare the Concordat of Worms (1122), and later converted much of Pomerania as a papal legate. He died at Bamberg on 30 June 1139 and was canonized in 1189.
b.s: The letters and diplomas held here document his conduct during the Investiture Controversy: bishops owe the emperor fidelity and military service while church property is immune from secular power, the king must protect and defend the churches, obedience is due to the pope and his legate, and the works polemicize against Emperor Henry V and his court.

w: Acts of the Assembly of Augsburg
Acts of the Assembly of Pavia
Acts of the Council of Ingelheim
Mandate concerning the enthronement of the Archbishop of Magdeburg

b.bio: Otto I, son of Henry I and Mathilda, succeeded his father as king of Germany in 936 and was crowned emperor by Pope John XII in Rome in 962. He suppressed rebellious dukes, defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955, and had conquered the Kingdom of Italy by 961, transforming the German church through royal appointments and subjecting its clergy to his authority. The works held here are not treatises but imperial documents: council acts from Ingelheim, Augsburg, Pavia and Frankfurt, a treaty with John XII, privileges, edicts, and the Roman coronation record. They show Otto acting on church affairs — proceedings against John XII and regulation of sees such as Magdeburg — asserting that divine law stands above human law and that spiritual arms precede temporal ones against the church's enemies.
b.s: These charters and council acts document how the Ottonian king exercised authority over councils, bishops, and even a pope, making them primary evidence for early imperial control of the church.

b.bio:
Otto I (912–973) — Otto I, son of Henry I and Mathilda, succeeded his father as king of Germany in 936 and was crowned emperor by Pope John XII in Rome in 962. He suppressed rebellious dukes, defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955, and had conquered the Kingdom of Italy by 961, transforming the German church through royal appointments and subjecting its clergy to his authority. The works held here are not treatises but imperial documents: council acts from Ingelheim, Augsburg, Pavia and Frankfurt, a treaty with John XII, privileges, edicts, and the Roman coronation record. They show Otto acting on church affairs — proceedings against John XII and regulation of sees such as Magdeburg — asserting that divine law stands above human law and that spiritual arms precede temporal ones against the church's enemies.

Otto II (955–983) — Otto II, called the Red, son of Otto I and Adelaide of Italy, was crowned German king in 961 and co-emperor in 967, ruling alone from his father's death in 973 until his death in Rome on 7 December 983. He married the Byzantine princess Theophanu on 14 April 972 and continued Ottonian control over the church. The two documents held here under his name are not theological works but acts of government: an edict on judicial procedure and a peace settlement with the Venetians.
b.s: These charters and council acts document how the Ottonian king exercised authority over councils, bishops, and even a pope, making them primary evidence for early imperial control of the church.

b.bio: Otto II, called the Red, son of Otto I and Adelaide of Italy, was crowned German king in 961 and co-emperor in 967, ruling alone from his father's death in 973 until his death in Rome on 7 December 983. He married the Byzantine princess Theophanu on 14 April 972 and continued Ottonian control over the church. The two documents held here under his name are not theological works but acts of government: an edict on judicial procedure and a peace settlement with the Venetians.
b.s: The pages here show imperial law regulating judicial combat, perjury, and ecclesiastical pleading through advocates — evidence of how civil magistracy and church procedure intersected under Ottonian rule.

b.bio: Otto III, son of Emperor Otto II and Theophanu, was elected German king in 983 at the age of three. After regencies under Henry II of Bavaria (whose claim failed in 984), his mother Theophanu (d. 991), and grandmother Adelaide (to 994), he took rule himself. In 996 he marched to Italy, was crowned emperor, suppressed a Roman revolt under Crescentius II, and installed his cousin as Pope Gregory V, the first pope of German descent. He died near Viterbo/Paterno in January 1002. The two documents held here — a constitution issued at Pavia and an edict — are imperial acts on church property: they deny that alienations of church goods bind successors, void laws and customs against the church's utility, and attach anathema to opponents.
b.s: The works here are imperial constitutions asserting that bishops may not bind successors by alienating church property and that laws against the church's utility are void — documents of Ottonian church-state policy relevant to the locus of the civil magistrate's relation to ecclesiastical goods.

b.bio: No surviving record here describes a person named Octavius Turcius; the biographical material provided concerns Marcus Minucius Felix, the Roman advocate and apologist of the second or third century who wrote the dialogue Octavius — a different author who must be kept apart from Octavius Turcius. What can be said of this name rests entirely on the library's holding: three pages of 'Preliminary Observations' printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 151, a piece of antiquarian-liturgical scholarship rather than patristic composition.
b.s: The single work held is a short scholarly preface treating the reverence shown to sacred books in the ancient church, the ornamentation of liturgical codices by monks, and the provenance of a Ravenna sacramentary of the mid-eleventh century.
